newsitem.title: INDIA: India might ease investment outflow curbs - paper.
newsitem.headline: India might ease investment outflow curbs - paper.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram was quoted on Wednesday as saying the government is considering relaxing restrictions on the outflow of investments to cope with rising foreign exchange reserves.

"We must do something constructive with our increasing dollar reserves, and one way of productively deploying them is to allow a more liberal outward investment flow," the Economic Times quoted Chidambaram as saying.

India's foreign exchange reserves, including gold and Special Drawing Rights, rose to $28.22 billion on June 6 from $21.66 billion one year earlier, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reported on Monday.

Currently, the RBI must clear overseas investments of $4 million or more on a case-by-case basis, the business daily said. In the 1996/97 fiscal year ended on March 31, a modest $350 million in overseas investments was approved, it said.
Chidambaram told the newspaper that the liberalisation of investment outflows was in line with the recommendations of a committee headed by former RBI deputy governor S.S. Tarapore.
Earlier this month the committee outlined steps the country needed to take to be able to float the rupee as a fully convertible currency by 2000.
The newspaper said the government would announce its policy towards investment outflows within a week.
Chidambaram said he would implement parts of the Tarapore report on the convertibility of the rupee when necessary conditions are met.
"For instance, I liberalised the external commercial borrowing policy for loans of over 10 years because as per the committee's recommendations the time was ripe to do so," he said.
Last week the government removed the ceiling on external commercial borrowings with maturities of more than 10 years.
"Similarly, as I go down the road I will implement more decisions provided the conditions state in the report are met," the finance minister was quoted as saying.
Chidambaram said burgeoning foreign exchange reserves needed to be used productively, and it was a matter of concern that growing dollar reserves were not being used to purchase more imports.

"My experience as the commerce minister suggests that higher exports are possible only if imports pick up substantially. This must necessarily happen to further fuel industrial growth," Chidambaram said.
He said excess dollars in the system must be used by "much higher imports of capital goods, intermediates and technology".
The finance minister said consumer imports could be liberalised but that alone would not lead to productive use of dollars.
